packs.title: Frames & Forms
packs.promise: Read Brussels through reflected shapes, small stories and a fossil clue.

q.s: Test how a window can show two places at once.
st: Choose a shop window from the public walking space without blocking its entrance.
Match three reflected shapes with the real objects or architectural details that seem to produce them. Describe each pair briefly.
Take a few safe paces to one side and test one match. Does the reflection move differently from the object behind the glass?
If reflections are faint, match three repeated fixed details along the arcade instead, then find one small difference between a pair.

q.s: Make a tiny story that works without a single spoken word.
st: Visit a permanent display about how comics are made, or read the museum’s linked account of comic-strip art. Focus on how one action can be divided into moments.
Invent a small everyday event with a beginning, change and result: a hat caught by wind, a dropped pencil or another event of your own.
Make three original wordless panels as simple shapes or describe exactly what each would show. Familiar comic characters are unnecessary.
Hide the middle panel. Decide what becomes unclear or more surprising, then restore or change it to improve the sequence.

q.s: See what one unbroken line can remember.
st: Choose a safe, comfortable place where you can see part of the garden and some building edges.
Trace one connected line across those shapes on paper, with a finger in the air or in a short spoken sequence. Do not lift your imaginary pen to include every detail.
Look away from the view and repeat the line from memory.
Compare the two versions. Circle or describe the feature that changed most, and decide whether it mattered to the feeling of the view.

packs.title: Marolles & Sablon
packs.promise: Give everyday objects, street textures and familiar paths a second look.

q.s: Put three secondhand objects to work in an imagined small problem.
st: Invent a simple practical need: organising a desk, setting up a tiny reading corner or another problem of your choice.
From the public walking space, choose three visible secondhand objects that could help. Look without handling them or interrupting a sale.
Explain how the three would work together. Give them new roles if useful, but keep any invented story clearly imaginary.
Remove one object from your plan. Decide what would stop working or what you could manage without.

q.s: Keep an object’s shape and change its purpose.
st: Choose one object with a distinctive physical feature: a handle, hollow, curve, hinge or another visible form.
Invent two new jobs for it while keeping that feature. The ideas may be playful, but distinguish them from the object’s real history or use.
Draw or describe both versions. Add just one imagined change to make your preferred version work better.
Give the preferred version a short invented name and explain why you chose it.

q.s: Use a stone outline to begin an original colour design.
st: Choose one pointed window outline visible from outside. Simplify its outer shape without trying to copy every stone division.
Fill that imagined frame with a pattern using only two colours, or two named tones if you have no drawing materials. Make the pattern your own.
Change the balance so one colour occupies much more space. Compare the result with your first version.
Choose the version you prefer and explain how its balance feels. You need not interpret or reproduce religious imagery.
